purpose: Evaluate whether proposed institutional strength, stress, adoption, conflict, and network variables predict institutional consolidation, fragmentation, and loss of top-level autonomy better than simpler alternatives.
nonGoal: This contract does not assume or attempt to prove that an Apex Institution must emerge.

primaryScope.population: Sovereign state-system members, including historical predecessors and successors where identifiers can be reconciled.
primaryScope.corporateScope: Deferred to a separately estimated corporate study after the state-only pipeline passes its gates.

outcomes.label: Any top-level institutional transition
outcomes.eventDefinition: First observed consolidation, subordination, fragmentation, dissolution, or recognized successor transition after the prediction origin.

outcomes.label: Institution gains top-level influence or members
outcomes.eventDefinition: A coded merger, federation, annexation, delegated-authority expansion, or successor transition that increases the Institution's top-level scope.

outcomes.label: Institution loses top-level autonomy
outcomes.eventDefinition: The Institution ceases to exercise independent highest-level authority through merger, annexation, dissolution, or durable delegation.

outcomes.label: Institution fragments
outcomes.eventDefinition: Two or more recognized successor Institutions acquire top-level autonomy from one predecessor.

outcomes.label: Institution dissolves without coded peer consolidation
outcomes.eventDefinition: The Institution exits the defined system without a single consolidated successor event.

outcomes.label: Institution adopts a common standard
outcomes.eventDefinition: Formal requirement plus a separately measured implementation or enforcement indicator.

outcomes.label: Lag from formal adoption to effective implementation
outcomes.eventDefinition: Elapsed time between formal adoption and the preregistered implementation threshold.

outcomes.label: Duration of an influence share above 50 percent
outcomes.eventDefinition: Time between first crossing above 50 percent and terminal consolidation, reversal below 50 percent, or right-censoring.

outcomes.label: One top-level Institution with majority effective implementation
outcomes.eventDefinition: Exactly one coded top-level Institution remains and effective implementation of its common standard exceeds 50 percent.

hypotheses.statement: Debt stress, inequality, and internal disorder increase fragmentation or loss-of-control hazard.
hypotheses.nullModel: Age/time baseline hazard with region and period strata but no stress variables.
hypotheses.falsification: Reject or revise if effects are absent, reverse sign across most held-out windows, are not calibrated, or fail to improve preregistered out-of-sample metrics.

hypotheses.statement: Relative productive, financial, and material strength predicts which Institution gains influence during restructuring.
hypotheses.falsification: Reject or simplify if the strength vector does not outperform size-only and historical-frequency baselines across held-out periods.

hypotheses.statement: Formal institutional consolidation or standard adoption precedes effective implementation by a measurable lag.
hypotheses.nullModel: Immediate implementation at the formal adoption date.
hypotheses.falsification: Reject the lag mechanism if implementation is indistinguishable from immediate adoption after accounting for reporting delay, or if estimated lags do not generalize across standards.

hypotheses.statement: As the field contracts below approximately 20 Institutions, effective power becomes comparatively balanced and influence above 50 percent is short-lived before terminal consolidation or reversal.
hypotheses.nullModel: Majority episodes have the same duration distribution as non-majority concentration episodes.
hypotheses.falsification: Reject the terminal-majority rule if stable 51–99 percent influence episodes are common and long-lived relative to comparable concentration episodes.

hypotheses.statement: Technical standardization can increase without producing top-level political or institutional consolidation.
hypotheses.nullModel: Technical adoption and institutional consolidation share one common transition process.
hypotheses.falsification: Reject independence if technical convergence consistently predicts rapid common top-level authority across held-out standards and periods.

hypotheses.statement: Big Cycle variables improve transition prediction beyond simpler power-transition and debt-only models.
hypotheses.nullModel: Constant hazard, debt-only, material-power-only, and power-transition-only models.
hypotheses.falsification: Reject the composite if it does not exceed the best simple baseline by the preregistered practical margin in rolling held-out tests.

hypotheses.statement: Multiplex network dependency predicts consolidation and subordination beyond direct economic or material size.
hypotheses.nullModel: Direct relative-size and geographic-distance model without network measures.
hypotheses.falsification: Reject the network mechanism if network variables add no stable held-out predictive value after direct size, distance, and period controls.

evaluationPolicy.splitStrategy: Rolling-origin temporal evaluation with the final interval held untouched until model selection is complete.
evaluationPolicy.selectionRule: A complex model advances only if it improves calibration or predictive score over the best simpler baseline by a preregistered practical margin in a majority of held-out windows.
evaluationPolicy.rightCensoring: Retain censoring indicators and event times. Never replace a non-event with the horizon as if it were observed, except clearly labeled exploratory diagnostics.
evaluationPolicy.rareEvents: Prefer precision-recall, calibrated probabilities, and proper scoring rules over accuracy.
evaluationPolicy.multipleTesting: Declare primary outcomes and adjust or label exploratory secondary analyses.
evaluationPolicy.negativeResults: Record null, unstable, and sign-reversing results in the same report as supportive results.

requirements: Every hypothesis has at least one prediction horizon.
Every hypothesis has a falsification condition.
Every hypothesis has named source identifiers or a documented evidence gap.
Censoring and leakage rules are explicit.
